Reading Order Reconstruction for Mobile Document
Readers
Alice Example
and Bob Sample
Example University
Abstract
Mobile readers struggle with documents that were typeset for paper. Two-column layouts, running
headers, and hyphenated line breaks make the text hard to follow on a narrow screen. We present a re-
construction technique that recovers the reading order of scholarly documents from the positions of
their glyphs and reflows the text so that it can be read comfortably on a telephone.
1 Introduction
Scholarly publishing still revolves around the portable
document format. Conference proceedings, technical re-
ports, and standards documents are distributed as fixed
layouts that faithfully reproduce the printed page. This fi-
delity comes at a price: on a small display the reader must
zoom, pan, and scroll in two dimensions to follow a sin-
gle sentence across a column boundary, which interrupts
concentration and makes careful reading of long specifi-
cations exhausting.
Our approach treats the document as a collection of
positioned words rather than as an image. By grouping
words into lines, lines into columns, and columns into a
reading sequence, the system recovers the logical flow of
the text. Figures, tables, and displayed equations are pre-
served as cropped images of the original page, because
their meaning depends on the arrangement that the author
chose.
The contributions of this paper are:
a reading order algorithm that handles two-column
pages and full-width titles;
a paragraph segmentation rule based on indentation
and spacing.
2 Design
The first stage collects every text fragment together with
its baseline, font size, and horizontal extent. Fragments
that share a baseline are merged into lines, and super-
scripts such as footnote markers are attached to the line
they decorate. A vertical gap that remains empty across
most of the page reveals the boundary between the two
columns, even when a wide title or a figure spanning both
columns crosses it.

The second stage decides where paragraphs begin.
Typeset documents signal a new paragraph either with
additional vertical space or with an indented first line.
Both cues are measured relative to the typical line spac-
ing of the body text, so the method adapts to documents
with different typographic conventions without manual
configuration.

2.1 Running Headers and Hyphenation
Running headers and page numbers repeat on every page
and carry no information for the reader. They are recog-
nized by comparing the text near the top and bottom mar-
gins across pages, ignoring the digits that change from
one page to the next. Hyphenated words at the end of a
line are rejoined unless the same hyphenated form ap-
pears elsewhere in the document, which preserves com-
pound words such as state-of-the-art techniques while re-
pairing words that were merely broken for justification.

3 Evaluation
We evaluated the reconstruction on a collection of con-
ference papers and technical reports. For each document
we compared the recovered paragraphs with the source
text and counted the paragraphs whose words appeared in
the correct order. The comparison was strict: a single
misplaced fragment caused the entire paragraph to be
counted as incorrect.

4 Conclusion
Reflowing fixed layouts is an old problem, but the com-
bination of glyph positions, font metrics, and simple sta-
tistics about the page is sufficient for the documents that
researchers read most often. The resulting text adapts to
the reader instead of forcing the reader to adapt to the
page.
